name: Real Estate

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.0% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the latest measured period, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making this one of the more consistently tracked adoption figures across sectors. The increase is modest but steady, and the Census data comes directly from firm responses rather than vendor estimates, giving it more credibility than many industry self-assessments.

The oldest and most consequential AI application in the sector is automated valuation. Zillow publishes Zestimate home valuations for over 110 million homes using a neural network model that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, listing signals, and user-submitted data, with updates running multiple times per week. HouseCanary covers over 136 million U.S. properties with AI-powered valuations, forecasts, and analytics, combining machine learning with image recognition that identifies room types and assesses home condition from photos. Opendoor deploys pricing models that carry direct balance-sheet exposure, having served over 307,753 homeowners through an iBuyer model where valuation errors translate immediately into financial losses. These systems represent AI with real capital consequences rather than productivity tooling.

That stakes profile is precisely why automated valuation models are now federally regulated. The CFPB, FHFA, OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized quality control standards under the Dodd-Frank Act requiring that institutions using AVMs in mortgage credit decisions or securitization adopt policies to ensure high confidence in estimates, protect against data manipulation, avoid conflicts of interest, and conduct random sample testing and reviews. This is the sector's first binding federal AI governance layer, and it applies across the mortgage origination and secondary market chain. Firms deploying or relying on AVMs in covered transactions must now treat model quality as a compliance obligation, not merely a product concern.

Beyond valuation, AI has moved into the operational fabric of both residential and commercial property management. EliseAI offers an agentic conversational platform that handles leasing inquiries, schedules tours, follows up with prospects, and manages maintenance requests around the clock, with the stated aim of reducing overhead and freeing staff for higher-value work. Prophia applies document AI to commercial lease abstraction, extracting key terms and rent-roll data from lease documents and combining that output with expert validation to produce structured data for portfolio management. Building Engines, a JLL company, offers an AI-powered property management platform called Prism that delivers recommendations and automation intended to cut costs and grow net operating income for commercial property teams. Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D models and integrates with Procore and Autodesk, positioning its computer-vision output as a data layer for portfolio management and construction workflows.

On the enterprise side, JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, applying it across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics. Compass integrates AI into residential brokerage workflows for agent productivity and client matching. The investment and startup ecosystem supporting these deployments includes CRETI, which connects over 500 investors focused on real estate technology, and NAR REACH, the technology scale-up program operated by Second Century Ventures, described as the most active venture fund in global real estate technology. CREtech convenes commercial real estate leaders around AI deployment, with its 2026 New York conference projecting 3,000 attendees and over 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings, a scale that reflects genuine industry organizing around the technology rather than peripheral interest.

A reader evaluating AI deployment in this sector should note that the regulatory environment is already active for the highest-stakes application, automated valuation in mortgage contexts, and compliance requirements there are non-negotiable for covered institutions. For operational applications such as leasing automation, lease abstraction, and building management, the sources collectively suggest that productivity and cost reduction are the primary pitch, though independently audited ROI figures do not appear in the available material. The Census figure of 28.0% adoption means roughly seven in ten firms in the sector have not yet reported active use, suggesting that for many organizations the decision is still ahead of them rather than behind.
